title: Wave-based capacity hedging and tenant backpressure controller for LTS rollouts
creator: Ava Martinez
description:
Background: Past LTS rollouts and forced GPU pool upgrades caused transient capacity crunches when many tenants were drained simultaneously or when autoscaler contracts reacted with latency. We need an upgrade mechanism that preserves per-tenant latency SLOs and minimizes customer-visible throttling during upgrades of dedicated GPU pools.

Proposal: Implement a Wave-based Capacity Hedging (WCH) controller that coordinates upgrade waves, banks headroom between waves, and exposes a Tenant Backpressure Controller (TBC) that provides per-tenant soft-throttles to avoid hotspots. Key features: 1) Wave reservations: controller reserves a hedging budget (headroom) before decommissioning nodes in each wave. 2) Rate-limited drain: pods/tenants are evicted with token-bucket fairness and tenant-priority weighting. 3) Autoscaler handshake: a deterministic API for autoscaler to claim/release hedging budget; autoscaler agrees to maintain min headroom during wave. 4) Backpressure signals: TBC emits temporary capacity signals to routers/dispatcher so load can be smoothed across tenants or redirected to fallback model variants. 5) Canary gating: small initial waves run canary traffic with tight SLO monitoring and automatic gate closure on regressions.

Design trade-offs: We prefer soft backpressure over hard evictions to reduce user-facing errors at the expense of slightly higher tail latency. Banking headroom reduces upgrade speed but substantially lowers customer impact. Integrating with autoscaler requires a small API change but avoids speculative overprovision.

Acceptance criteria: 1) No increase in 99th percentile serving latency >10% for affected tenants during staged upgrades in canary testing. 2) Successful end-to-end upgrade with 95% of tenants experiencing zero error rate increase in integration testbed. 3) Autoscaler handshake implemented and covered by unit/integration tests. 4) Runbook and dashboard available for on-call.

Migration plan: Implement WCH and TBC as opt-in feature flags on a single dedicated fleet for initial validation. Run two staged upgrades (internal traffic, then a slice of customer traffic). If successful, enable in small percentage of fleets before full rollout.

Risks and mitigations: 1) Misconfigured hedging budget -> slow upgrades: mitigate with safety timeouts and operator override. 2) Backpressure causing user confusion: provide clear console signals and telemetry. 3) Autoscaler incompatibility: fallback to conservative draining behavior if handshake unavailable.
